items.q: Do you have regular personnel, or is the band filled with whoever is available?
items.a: The contract names a configuration: the size, the instrumentation and the repertoire, and that is exactly what performs on your date. Behind it, every act on the roster is an existing group with its own repertoire and its own regular personnel, and a named act is published under the name of the person who fronts it. Any substitution, the front included, is named to you in advance along with the reason. A flamenco act is not assembled out of whoever was free, and a funk act is never asked to play dinner volume it does not play.

items.q: What happens if a player cannot make the date?
items.a: Any substitution is named to you in advance. Subs are how every roster in this business works; the part that goes wrong is a planner discovering one at load-in. You get the name and the reason as soon as we know, which is the promise we can actually keep.

items._rewritten_note: 2026-08-17. Daniel: the contact's role does not matter to the client, so the player-not-coordinator claim and the two-roles explanation are gone. The answer is now exactly what the contract promises: a name and mobile in writing two weeks out, reachable load-in to load-out.
items.q: Who do we deal with on the night?
items.a: One named person. You get their name and mobile number in writing before the event, and they are reachable from load-in to load-out.

items._closed_note: Closed 2026-08-17. Daniel: no showcases, and these are private groups that do not play public dates, so the first version's offer to point at a public date was wrong too. The honest answer is no, and it is written as a straight no rather than a hedge. NOTE: this makes video the only pre-booking evidence that can ever exist, which moves the footage shoots from nice-to-have to the answer to a question every planner asks.
items.q: Can we see the band play before we book?
items.a: No. These are private-event groups. They do not play public dates you could attend, and we do not stage showcases, because a showcase is a performance for an audience that came to judge it. Video on each act's page is the substitute, alongside paperwork you can check before you commit to anything.

items.q: What do the players wear?
items.a: Black tie, business formal or all black, whichever your event calls for. Tell us the dress code you have set for guests and we will sit one notch inside it. If you need something specific, put it in the contract and that is what the players wear.

items._closed_note: Closed 2026-08-16 against contract §3. Vocabulary aligned to the contract: deposit, not retainer. The net-30 exception was missing here and is in the contract.
items.q: What holds a date?
items.a: A signed contract and a deposit, both at booking. Until both land the date stays available to anyone else asking for it, and we will tell you if someone does. Approved corporate accounts on net-30 are the exception: those hold on signature, and the fee is invoiced after the event.

items._closed_note: Closed 2026-08-16 against contract §3 and the invoice format in readiness/03c. Card was pulled that day because no processor existed; Daniel confirmed Stripe 2026-08-17 and it is restored. Fee decision 2026-08-17: Signet absorbs the card processing fee, so all three methods cost the client the same. ACH remit details still pend the bank conversation, which pends the trade-name filing.
items.q: When is the balance due, and how do we pay?
items.a: The balance is due 14 days before the event. ACH, a check made out to the name on the contract, or card through Stripe, all at no fee. Every method costs you the same, so pick whichever your finance process prefers. Corporate clients can be approved for net-30 instead, invoiced at the event and due 30 days after it, with a purchase order number on the invoice if your finance team uses one.

items._closed_note: CLOSED 2026-08-17 at 90 days, Daniel's call, and contract §5 now says the same. History: the site originally said 90 days but framed the retainer as transferring, which contradicted the contract draft's 30-day line and its separate free postponement. Reconciled to the contract on 16 Aug at 30, then the 30 was rejected as too generous: a date released inside 90 days cannot realistically be resold, which is the whole reason the date is held. The free postponement is what keeps this fair, so this only bites on a genuine cancellation.
items.q: What is the cancellation policy?
items.a: Postponing is almost always cheaper than cancelling and we will say so at the time. One move to a new date inside twelve months is free, subject to availability, and everything paid transfers. If we cannot make any date that works, you get everything back. A straight cancellation more than 90 days out costs the deposit and nothing further. At 90 days or fewer the fee is due, less any travel and lodging we have not already spent. Ninety days is the line because a date released inside it is one we cannot realistically fill again, and holding your date meant turning other work away. If we ever cancel on you, you get everything back and we help you find the replacement.

items.q: Do you carry liability insurance?
items.a: Yes. A certificate naming your venue as additional insured comes in the same email as the contract, along with a W-9 and one itemised invoice. You do not have to ask for any of them.

items.q: Can you work with our procurement or AP process?
items.a: Yes. We can be set up as a vendor, quote against a purchase order, and invoice in whatever form your finance team needs. Ask early; vendor onboarding is usually the slowest thing on a corporate booking.

items.q: How far in advance should we book?
items.a: Corporate holiday parties are typically decided August through October for November and December dates, and New Year's Eve books earliest of all. Weddings and galas run longer: ten to twelve months, and twelve to eighteen for a mountain venue or a fall Saturday.

items.q: How long are the sets, and how long are the breaks?
items.a: Sets run 45 to 60 minutes with 15 to 20 minutes between them, set against your run of show rather than a fixed clock. Audio continues through every break at every size, so the night never goes silent.

items.q: Can we use your microphones for speeches?
items.a: Yes. A dedicated announcement microphone is on its own channel at every size, live from the moment we finish sound check. Hand it to whoever is speaking. No cable swap, no gap, no borrowing the singer's mic.

items.q: Will you learn a song we choose?
items.a: The first one is included in every booking. Each one after that is its own line on the quote. Send it at least four weeks out, with the version you mean; there are usually several and they are not the same chart.

items.q: Do you make announcements or act as MC?
items.a: The bandleader will make short announcements from the stage: dinner is served, the dance floor is open, please welcome your speaker. We do not run the evening as an MC. If your program needs a host, that is a separate hire and we will work to their cues.

items.q: Can we add time on the night?
items.a: Yes, and it costs what the earlier hours cost. There is no overtime rate. Added time bills at the same figure the earlier hours did, in 30-minute increments, agreed on the night with whoever holds the budget, so the only question at 11pm is whether the crowd wants one more.

items.q: How loud is it, really?
items.a: Dinner and cocktails run 65 to 72 dBA at the nearest table, which is a volume you can talk across without raising your voice. Dancing runs 88 to 95 dBA on the floor. If your venue enforces a cap, tell us the number at contract and we will build the night under it rather than argue about it at 10pm.

items.q: Do you provide sound and lighting?
items.a: Sound sized to the venue is included at every size. Stage lighting and a dedicated front-of-house engineer are optional add-ons, quoted as their own line. We do not light the space, the tables or a dance floor as a design element; that is your lighting vendor's work, and we will coordinate with them.

items._note: ADDED 2026-08-27 from a buyer-questions pass. Daniel's phrasing: 'We take care of that unless you or the hotel has hired an additional contractor for sound support, in which case that would be their domain.' Downtown hotels commonly carry mandatory in-house AV (Encore and similar), so this is a real corporate-buyer question the site did not answer.
items.q: The venue has its own AV company. Whose sound system runs the night?
items.a: Ours, unless you or the venue have hired a sound contractor, in which case sound support is their domain: we advance the plan with them before the night and play through what they run. Either way it is settled at contract rather than at load-in.

items.q: Do you need a stage, and do you provide one?
items.a: We do not require one and we do not supply one. A band plays fine on a floor. If you want a riser, the venue or your production company provides it, and the footprints we need at each size are published on the technical page.

items.q: What power do you need?
items.a: Dedicated 20-amp circuits within reach of the stage, one or two of them depending on the size of the band. The requirement most often missed is that they be dedicated: sharing a circuit with catering warmers or a lighting truss is the single most common cause of a problem at load-in. Exact counts are on the technical page.

items._closed_note: Closed 2026-08-16 against contract §7, which requires a covered, level, dry performance area. Level and dry were missing here.
items.q: Can you play outdoors?
items.a: Yes, on a covered, level and dry performance area, with power run to it and a plan for the weather written before the day. Colorado evenings drop fast, and instruments and electronics both stop behaving in the cold and the wet. Cover is not optional and neither is a defined move-indoors call time.

items.q: The venue has a curfew and a decibel limit. Is that a problem?
items.a: No. Mountain and residential venues run on their own rules and we honour them as written. Tell us the cap and the curfew when you book and both go into the plan, including how the last twenty minutes are shaped so the night ends on a high note rather than a cut-off.

items._closed_note: Closed 2026-08-17. Daniel: green room not needed but it supports their event; if meals are served the band would like them. The old answer made both a requirement over four hours. Because neither is an obligation, this does NOT go into contract §7, which cancels draft note 7 on 03a.
items.q: Do the players need a green room or meals?
items.a: Neither is a requirement. A green room, where one exists, does more for your event than for us: it keeps cases and spare gear out of your guests' sightline and gives the band somewhere to change that is not a corridor. On meals, we do not ask for them. If meals are being served, the band would like them, and a vendor meal is exactly right.

items.q: How much say do we get over the songs?
items.a: As much or as little as you want. You can build the list yourself, hand us a do-not-play list and leave the rest, or describe the crowd and let the band read it song by song. Most clients do the middle one, and the do-not-play list is the part worth spending time on.

items.q: Do you take requests during the event?
items.a: From you, yes, and from guests where it fits. The bandleader's job is reading the floor, so a request that would empty it gets a straight answer and an alternative rather than a yes and a bad twenty minutes.

faqs.q: What does a band cost for a corporate event in Denver?
faqs.a: In this market a cover or jazz band for a corporate event runs {{market:us_corporate_band}}, and the four to six piece build the Denver market treats as its middle runs {{market:denver_midtier_band}}. Those are the market's figures, not ours. Signet prices the date you are asking about, because a Tuesday in September and a Saturday in December are not the same job.

No. What is published here is what live music costs in this market, each figure with the source it was read from, so a budget can be set before anyone writes to us. The number for your night comes back when you send the date, and it accounts for the size, the hours, the venue and the drive.

Most acts in this market bill two things: a call-out that covers the evening they commit to whatever its length, and an hourly rate for performance time. That is why a one-hour cocktail set is not a quarter of a four-hour reception. Sound sits inside the figure with some acts and arrives as its own line with others, which is the first thing worth checking when two quotes look far apart.

faqs.q: Do you provide a certificate of insurance?
faqs.a: Yes, naming your venue as additional insured, sent in the same email as the contract. The limits are the pair Colorado venues write into their vendor requirements. A W-9 and one itemised invoice come with it.

faqs.q: Can one booking cover cocktails and dancing?
faqs.a: Yes. Once we are in the building the setup is already paid for, so a smaller group covering ceremony, cocktails or dinner alongside the main booking is a cheaper way to cover the night than hiring twice. One contract, one load-in, one invoice.
